entries.meaning: To start doing something, or to start happening — the neutral everyday word for the opening of an action, a period, or a process.
examples: We begin the meeting at nine every Monday.
She began studying Portuguese last spring.
He has begun writing his second novel.
He begins every class the same way.
The rain began just as we left the house.
By the time we arrived, the ceremony had begun.
Flu season begins earlier every year.
Every chapter begins with a quotation.
The tour began with a walk through the old town.
Tickets begin at forty dollars.
To begin with, the numbers in this report don't add up.
The engine was noisy to begin with, and it only got worse.
I cannot begin to thank you for what you did.
That settlement doesn't begin to cover the damage.
Nothing had begun to prepare us for the noise.

senses.head: Start doing something
body: The core transitive sense, also used with to + verb or with the -ing form; the two are interchangeable in most contexts. Slightly more formal than start, which is the default in speech. (начинать, приниматься за)
examples: We begin the meeting at nine every Monday.
She began studying Portuguese last spring.
He has begun writing his second novel.
He begins every class the same way.

senses.head: Start to happen, get under way
body: Intransitive, with an event, season, or process as the subject. Remember that begun never stands alone as a past — ✗ the show begun late. (начинаться)
examples: The rain began just as we left the house.
By the time we arrived, the ceremony had begun.
Flu season begins earlier every year.

senses.head: begin with — have as its first part
body: Used of lists, words, books, journeys — anything with an order. The related begin at gives a starting point on a scale or a price. (начинаться с)
examples: Every chapter begins with a quotation.
The tour began with a walk through the old town.
Tickets begin at forty dollars.

senses.head: to begin with (fixed phrase)
body: A frozen infinitive used as a sentence adverb, meaning either 'first of all' when listing reasons or 'at the outset' when saying how something originally was. Not a live use of the verb. (во-первых; для начала; изначально)
examples: To begin with, the numbers in this report don't add up.
The engine was noisy to begin with, and it only got worse.

senses.head: not begin to — not come close to
body: Emphatic and negative only. Cannot begin to means the speaker falls hopelessly short, not that they have failed to start. (даже близко не; и близко не)
examples: I cannot begin to thank you for what you did.
That settlement doesn't begin to cover the damage.
Nothing had begun to prepare us for the noise.

entries.register: everyday — one of the first verbs a learner meets and an American never stops using
entries.contrast: The past began and the participle begun are the two forms learners swap. Begun never stands alone as a past tense — ✗ I begun the report — it needs have: I have begun the report.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every live sense, of starting something (we begin the meeting) or of something starting (the rain began). Not stative, not linking; the frozen to begin with is a sentence adverb, not a working verb.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in sense 1 (we begin the meeting, also begin to study / begin studying), intransitive in sense 2 (the rain began, flu season begins earlier). The object is optional; begin with / begin at take a prepositional phrase, not an object.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the new wing was begun in 1890, the report has been begun but not finished; it sounds formal, and American speech usually reaches for started. No passive of the intransitive the ceremony had begun.

entries.meaning: To widen the mouth of a drilled hole, or to seat a fastener in it, so that the head sits flush with or below the surface; shop and machining vocabulary.
examples: Always countersink the pilot holes before you drive the screws.
He countersank each hole so the hinge would sit flat against the door.
The shop has countersunk every fastener on the panel.
Countersink the bolts so nothing catches on the deck.
By lunch we had countersunk all forty screws in the frame.
She countersinks the heads whenever the surface is going to be painted.

senses.head: Bevel a hole for a screw head
body: The core sense: cut a cone-shaped recess at the top of a pilot hole, usually with a countersink bit. Technical register — you will meet it in woodworking, metalwork, and assembly instructions, and almost nowhere else. (зенковать, раззенковывать (отверстие))
examples: Always countersink the pilot holes before you drive the screws.
He countersank each hole so the hinge would sit flat against the door.
The shop has countersunk every fastener on the panel.

senses.head: Set a fastener flush or below the surface
body: Said of the screw or bolt rather than of the hole. The participle countersunk doubles as the ordinary adjective — a countersunk screw — which is why the past countersank can look invented to people who have only seen the adjective. (утапливать (головку винта, болта))
examples: Countersink the bolts so nothing catches on the deck.
By lunch we had countersunk all forty screws in the frame.
She countersinks the heads whenever the surface is going to be painted.

entries.register: rare — shop and machining vocabulary; most people know only the adjective countersunk
entries.contrast: This is sink with a prefix, so it changes exactly the way sink does. The wrinkle is that countersunk is also the everyday adjective — a countersunk screw — so it is the form most people have seen, and the past countersank can look invented. It is not: he countersank the holes, he has countersunk the holes. Shop and machining vocabulary; you will rarely meet it elsewhere.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a physical shop operation on a hole or a fastener. No stative or linking use; the participle countersunk doubles as an ordinary adjective (a countersunk screw).
entries.transitivity: transitive in both senses, and the object is obligatory — either the hole (countersink the pilot holes) or the fastener (countersink the bolts). ✗ He countersank all morning is incomplete without one.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the commonest form in shop writing — every fastener on the panel has been countersunk, the holes were countersunk before assembly (never ✗ were countersank). The passive blurs into the adjective: the screws are countersunk.

entries.meaning: To take liquid into the mouth and swallow it — and, with no object, to consume alcohol.
examples: I drink coffee only in the morning.
She drank the whole bottle of water in one go.
He had drunk two cups before the meeting even started.
He doesn't drink.
They drank steadily all through the reception.
She has drunk nothing stronger than seltzer in ten years.
Let's drink to the happy couple.
We drank to absent friends and then sat down.
She stood at the rail and drank in the view.
The crowd drank in every word of his speech.
He has drunk in the applause all season.
Drink up — the cab is here.
They drank up and headed for the door.

senses.head: Swallow liquid
body: The neutral core sense, transitive or intransitive. Drank is the past and drunk the participle — ✗ I drunk the whole bottle is one of the most common slips in English. (пить)
examples: I drink coffee only in the morning.
She drank the whole bottle of water in one go.
He had drunk two cups before the meeting even started.

senses.head: Consume alcohol
body: With no object, drink means specifically to drink alcohol, often as a habit. The participle drunk is also the adjective for intoxicated — he was drunk — and before a noun that adjective becomes drunken: a drunken argument. (пить, употреблять спиртное)
examples: He doesn't drink.
They drank steadily all through the reception.
She has drunk nothing stronger than seltzer in ten years.

senses.head: drink to — raise a toast
body: Fixed with to; also drink a toast to. The standalone I'll drink to that means wholehearted agreement and needs no actual glass. (пить за (кого-л., что-л.))
examples: Let's drink to the happy couple.
We drank to absent friends and then sat down.

senses.head: drink in — take in eagerly
body: Figurative, of a view, an atmosphere, or someone's words. Slightly literary but common in descriptive prose and journalism. (упиваться, жадно впитывать)
examples: She stood at the rail and drank in the view.
The crowd drank in every word of his speech.
He has drunk in the applause all season.

senses.head: drink up — finish off a drink
body: Usually an imperative urging someone to hurry and finish. The related drink something down means to swallow it quickly, often unwillingly. (допивать (до дна))
examples: Drink up — the cab is here.
They drank up and headed for the door.

entries.register: everyday — as ordinary as eat, from the kitchen table to the wedding toast
entries.contrast: Drank is the past and drunk the participle — ✗ I drunk the whole bottle is one of the most common slips in English. Drunk is also the adjective meaning intoxicated (he was drunk), and before a noun that adjective becomes drunken (a drunken argument). Keep the participle where it belongs: after have, has, or had.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, from the literal swallowing to the figurative drink in the view. No stative or linking use; the intoxicated he was drunk is the adjective, not the verb.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the liquid as object (she drank the whole bottle, he drank in every word), intransitive in the alcohol sense (he doesn't drink, they drank all through the reception). The object is optional; drink to takes a prepositional phrase.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the whole bottle was drunk before dinner, his words were drunk in by the crowd (stiff but grammatical). Watch the clash with the adjective: the wine was drunk reads as the passive, the guests were drunk as intoxication. No passive of intransitive he doesn't drink.
entries.phrasal verbs: drink away · drink in · drink to · drink up

entries.meaning: To make, or to cause, a clear bell-like sound — and by extension to resound, to telephone, or to strike the ear as true or false.
examples: The church bells ring at noon every Sunday.
She rang the doorbell twice and waited on the porch.
My phone has rung four times this morning.
The hall rang with laughter.
My ears have rung ever since the concert.
A single shot rang out across the valley.
That name rings a bell, but I can't place it.
The address rang a bell the moment she said it.
His apology didn't ring true.
Every promise in that speech rang hollow.
Her account has rung true with everyone who has heard it.
The cashier rang up our groceries in under a minute.
The film has rung up three hundred million worldwide.
Ring me when you land, love. (British)
He rang her twice from the station. (British)
Police ringed the building before dawn.
Researchers have ringed every chick in the colony.

senses.head: Sound a bell, phone, or alarm
body: Works both ways: the bell rings, and a person rings the bell. The plain past is rang — ✗ I rung the doorbell. (звонить; звенеть)
examples: The church bells ring at noon every Sunday.
She rang the doorbell twice and waited on the porch.
My phone has rung four times this morning.

senses.head: Resound, be filled with sound
body: Of a place full of noise (usually ring with), of ears after something loud, or of a sound that carries (ring out). (звенеть; оглашаться; раздаваться)
examples: The hall rang with laughter.
My ears have rung ever since the concert.
A single shot rang out across the valley.

senses.head: ring a bell — sound familiar
body: Idiomatic, and always vague — you half remember but cannot place it. The subject is normally a name, a title, or a fact. (напоминать что-то, казаться знакомым)
examples: That name rings a bell, but I can't place it.
The address rang a bell the moment she said it.

senses.head: ring true / false / hollow
body: Of a statement, excuse, or apology: strike the listener as genuine or not. The complement is a fixed short list — true, false, hollow. (звучать правдиво / фальшиво / неубедительно)
examples: His apology didn't ring true.
Every promise in that speech rang hollow.
Her account has rung true with everyone who has heard it.

senses.head: ring up — total a sale
body: American retail usage: enter a purchase on the register. Extended to totals in general — a studio rings up box-office millions. (пробивать (на кассе); набирать сумму)
examples: The cashier rang up our groceries in under a minute.
The film has rung up three hundred million worldwide.

senses.head: ring someone — call by phone
body: British and Australian, not American: an American says call. The same varieties use ring up and ring back the same way. (звонить кому-л. по телефону)
examples: Ring me when you land, love. (British)
He rang her twice from the station. (British)

senses.head: Encircle, put a band on — regular verb
body: A separate verb that only shares the spelling, and it is completely regular: ring, ringed, ringed. Never ✗ rang in this sense. (окружать; кольцевать)
examples: Police ringed the building before dawn.
Researchers have ringed every chick in the colony.

entries.register: everyday — bells, phones, and alarms ring all day in ordinary American speech
entries.contrast: Two different verbs share this spelling. The bell verb is irregular — ring, rang, rung — but the verb meaning "encircle" or "put a ring on" is perfectly regular: police ringed the building, the biologist ringed the bird's leg. Within the bell verb, watch the usual swap: ✗ I rung the doorbell. The plain past is rang.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the bell, phone, and resounding senses; also linking (copular) in the fixed ring true / false / hollow, where an adjective complement follows instead of an object (his apology didn't ring true). The separate encircling verb (ring, ringed, ringed) is dynamic too.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when the bell or phone is the subject (my phone has rung four times, the hall rang with laughter), transitive when a person rings something (she rang the doorbell, the cashier rang up our groceries, British he rang her twice). The linking ring true takes a complement, not an object.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the bell was rung at noon, our groceries were rung up in under a minute. No passive of the intransitive the phone rang or of the linking use: ✗ true was rung by his apology.
entries.phrasal verbs: ring back · ring in · ring off · ring out · ring up

entries.meaning: To get smaller — in size, in quantity, or in nerve — or to make something smaller.
examples: Wool sweaters shrink if you wash them in hot water.
My favorite T-shirt shrank two sizes in the dryer.
The lake has shrunk every summer for a decade.
The company shrinks its inventory every January.
They shrank the logo so it would fit on the label.
Two rounds of layoffs have shrunk the department by half.
The economy shrank for two straight quarters.
Their lead had shrunk to three points by halftime.
He never shrinks from a hard conversation.
She has never shrunk from telling people exactly what she thinks.
The dog shrank back when he raised his hand.
The child shrinks into the corner whenever visitors arrive.

senses.head: Get smaller, contract
body: Especially of fabric in heat or water. American English accepts shrank and shrunk as the past, with shrank preferred in edited writing; the participle is always shrunk, and shrunken is an adjective only — ✗ it has shrunken. (садиться, сжиматься, уменьшаться)
examples: Wool sweaters shrink if you wash them in hot water.
My favorite T-shirt shrank two sizes in the dryer.
The lake has shrunk every summer for a decade.

senses.head: Make something smaller
body: Transitive: deliberately reduce a size, a budget, a staff, or an image on a screen. (сокращать, уменьшать)
examples: The company shrinks its inventory every January.
They shrank the logo so it would fit on the label.
Two rounds of layoffs have shrunk the department by half.

senses.head: Decline in amount or value
body: The standard word in economic and statistical writing for a quantity going down over time. (сокращаться, падать (об объёме, доходах))
examples: The economy shrank for two straight quarters.
Their lead had shrunk to three points by halftime.

senses.head: shrink from — avoid out of reluctance
body: Figurative, of duties, conflict, or hard truths, and most often negative — never shrinks from. (уклоняться от, страшиться, избегать)
examples: He never shrinks from a hard conversation.
She has never shrunk from telling people exactly what she thinks.

senses.head: Draw back, cower
body: Physical recoil from fear or pain, normally with back, away, or into. (съёживаться, отпрянуть, вжаться)
examples: The dog shrank back when he raised his hand.
The child shrinks into the corner whenever visitors arrive.

entries.register: everyday — sweaters, budgets, and economies all shrink; heard constantly
entries.contrast: American English accepts two pasts. Shrank is the one edited prose prefers — the sweater shrank in the dryer — while shrunk is common in speech and in titles like Honey, I Shrunk the Kids. The participle is always shrunk: it has shrunk. Shrunken is an adjective only — a shrunken head — never ✗ it has shrunken.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and an ergative pair: the same verb names the change of state (the sweater shrank) and the causing of it (they shrank the logo). No stative or linking use — shrunken is an adjective only, never ✗ it has shrunken.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive when the thing gets smaller or a person recoils (the lake has shrunk, the economy shrank, the dog shrank back, he never shrinks from a hard conversation), transitive when someone reduces it (the company shrinks its inventory, they shrank the logo).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the department has been shrunk by half, the image was shrunk to fit the label. No passive of the intransitive the lake has shrunk, and none of shrink from: ✗ the conversation was shrunk from.

entries.meaning: To produce musical sounds with the voice — and figuratively to make any clear ringing sound, or to talk when you were supposed to keep quiet.
examples: We sing the same two songs at every family birthday.
She sang the national anthem before the game.
That choir has sung in this hall for thirty years.
The lullaby was sung so quietly I almost missed it.
Cardinals sing outside the window all morning.
The kettle sang on the back burner.
The whole theater sang along with the chorus.
By the third verse everyone had sung along at least once.
They were sure he would sing once the deal was on the table.
One of the crew sang, and the whole case came together.
Her old boss sings her praises to anyone who asks.
Every review has sung the restaurant's praises.

senses.head: Produce music with the voice
body: The core sense, transitive or not, covering everything from humming in the shower to performing on stage. Sang is the past; sung belongs after have, has, had, and in the passive. (петь)
examples: We sing the same two songs at every family birthday.
She sang the national anthem before the game.
That choir has sung in this hall for thirty years.
The lullaby was sung so quietly I almost missed it.

senses.head: (Of birds or things) make a musical sound
body: Of birds, kettles, wind, and telephone wires — any clear sustained tone. Intransitive. (петь (о птицах); свистеть, звенеть)
examples: Cardinals sing outside the window all morning.
The kettle sang on the back burner.

senses.head: sing along — join in
body: With along or along with, of joining a song already in progress. The related sing out means to call something loudly. (подпевать)
examples: The whole theater sang along with the chorus.
By the third verse everyone had sung along at least once.

senses.head: Inform on someone (slang)
body: Crime-story slang: talk to the police about your accomplices. Intransitive, often sing to the cops. (сдать сообщников, «запеть»)
examples: They were sure he would sing once the deal was on the table.
One of the crew sang, and the whole case came together.

senses.head: sing someone's praises
body: Fixed phrase only: praise someone warmly and publicly, usually to a third party. (расхваливать, петь дифирамбы)
examples: Her old boss sings her praises to anyone who asks.
Every review has sung the restaurant's praises.

entries.register: everyday — the plain word for what a voice, a bird, or a kettle does
entries.contrast: Sang is the past, sung the participle. ✗ She sung at the wedding is wrong for a plain past — that is she sang. Sung belongs after have, has, or had, and in the passive: the anthem was sung by a local choir.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, whether a voice, a bird, a kettle, or an informer is the subject. No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: both, and ditransitive in one pattern — transitive with the song as object (she sang the national anthem), ditransitive with a hearer added (sing me a lullaby / sing a lullaby to me), intransitive in the bird, informer, and sing along senses (cardinals sing outside the window, one of the crew sang). The object is optional.
entries.passive: yes, and it is common — the anthem was sung by a local choir, the lullaby was sung so quietly I almost missed it. No passive of the intransitive senses: ✗ it was sung by the kettle.

entries.meaning: To go down — beneath water, to a lower level, or into a worse state — and, transitively, to drive or send something downward.
examples: Stones sink; driftwood floats.
The ferry sank in under twenty minutes.
Divers found a freighter that had sunk in 1904.
A single torpedo sank the destroyer.
Storms have sunk more boats on this coast than any war.
The sun sinks behind the ridge around seven.
The old porch has sunk three inches on the east side.
She sank into the armchair without a word.
Property values have sunk since the plant closed.
My heart had sunk before he finished the sentence.
He sank into a depression that winter.
The town has sunk into a slow decline since the mill closed.
Crews sink the posts four feet into the clay.
The dog sank its teeth into the rope toy.
They have sunk two new wells since the drought.
It took a week for the news to sink in.
The verdict had finally sunk in by the time she reached the car.
They sank half a million into that restaurant.
He has sunk every spare dollar into the boat.
She sinks twenty-foot putts like they're nothing.
He sank the free throw with two seconds left.

senses.head: Go under water, go down
body: The core sense. Sank is the standard past — sunk is heard in American speech but edited prose keeps sank. The participle is always sunk; sunken is an adjective only, as in a sunken living room. (тонуть, погружаться, идти ко дну)
examples: Stones sink; driftwood floats.
The ferry sank in under twenty minutes.
Divers found a freighter that had sunk in 1904.

senses.head: Send a ship to the bottom
body: Transitive, with a torpedo, a storm, or a crew scuttling its own vessel as the agent. (потопить, топить)
examples: A single torpedo sank the destroyer.
Storms have sunk more boats on this coast than any war.

senses.head: Drop to a lower level or position
body: Of the sun, of ground and buildings settling, or of a body lowering itself — usually with behind, below, or into. (опускаться, оседать, садиться (о солнце))
examples: The sun sinks behind the ridge around seven.
The old porch has sunk three inches on the east side.
She sank into the armchair without a word.

senses.head: Fall in value, amount, or spirits
body: Figurative decline — prices, ratings, hopes. My heart sank is the fixed English way of saying a hope collapsed in an instant. (падать, снижаться; упасть (о сердце, настроении))
examples: Property values have sunk since the plant closed.
My heart had sunk before he finished the sentence.

senses.head: sink into — pass into a state
body: Of sleep, silence, despair, debt, or decay: a gradual slide into a deeper or worse condition. (погружаться, впадать (в сон, отчаяние, долги))
examples: He sank into a depression that winter.
The town has sunk into a slow decline since the mill closed.

senses.head: Drive something down into a surface
body: Transitive: posts into ground, teeth into food, a well into rock. This is the sense the derived verb countersink is built on. (вбивать, вонзать, погружать)
examples: Crews sink the posts four feet into the clay.
The dog sank its teeth into the rope toy.
They have sunk two new wells since the drought.

senses.head: sink in — be fully understood
body: Of news or a fact registering after a delay. Intransitive and always with in. (доходить (до сознания), укладываться в голове)
examples: It took a week for the news to sink in.
The verdict had finally sunk in by the time she reached the car.

senses.head: sink money into — invest, often wastefully
body: Informal, and usually implying the money is gone or the return is doubtful. Related: sunk cost, money already spent and unrecoverable. (вбухать, вложить (деньги) — часто впустую)
examples: They sank half a million into that restaurant.
He has sunk every spare dollar into the boat.

senses.head: sink a putt or a shot
body: Sports usage — golf, pool, basketball: put the ball exactly where it is meant to go. (закатить, забить (мяч в лунку, в корзину))
examples: She sinks twenty-foot putts like they're nothing.
He sank the free throw with two seconds left.

entries.register: everyday — boats, hearts, and free throws; used without a second thought
entries.contrast: Sank is the standard past — the boat sank — but sunk is also acceptable in American English and turns up often in speech (the boat sunk); edited prose keeps sank. The participle is always sunk: the boat has sunk. Sunken is an adjective only: a sunken living room, sunken ships.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and an ergative pair: it names the going down (the ferry sank) and the sending down (a torpedo sank the destroyer). No stative or linking use — sunken is an adjective only, as in a sunken living room.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the downward senses (stones sink, the sun sinks behind the ridge, my heart sank, the news finally sank in), transitive in the causative and idiomatic ones (sank the destroyer, sink the posts four feet, sank half a million into that restaurant, sank the free throw).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the destroyer was sunk by a single torpedo, two new wells have been sunk since the drought, the putt was sunk with two seconds left. No passive of the intransitive the ferry sank or it took a week to sink in.

entries.meaning: To move suddenly and elastically — to leap, to snap, to burst into being — and to produce something on someone without warning.
examples: Cats spring onto the counter the second you turn around.
He sprang out of his chair when the phone rang.
The goalie has sprung left on every shot tonight.
Old hinges spring back harder than new ones.
The trap sprang the moment he touched the bait.
The screen door had sprung shut behind her.
New coffee shops have sprung up all over the neighborhood.
Tent cities sprang up along the highway within a week.
The whole project sprang from a conversation at lunch.
Her caution springs from years of being burned.
Two creeks have sprung from that hillside for as long as anyone remembers.
She springs the same question on me every year.
They sprang a surprise inspection on the whole department.
The old boat sprang a leak two miles out.
The roof has sprung a leak over the kitchen again.
His brother sprang him on bail the same night.
We have sprung her from the clinic a day early.

senses.head: Jump, leap suddenly
body: A quick movement from a standing or crouching start. Edited American prose prefers sprang, but sprung is widely used in speech and is not an error. (прыгать, вскакивать, бросаться)
examples: Cats spring onto the counter the second you turn around.
He sprang out of his chair when the phone rang.
The goalie has sprung left on every shot tonight.

senses.head: Snap shut or fly open by elastic force
body: Of doors, traps, latches, and springs releasing stored tension. The adjective sprung describes a mattress or a suspension that has lost its bounce. (распрямляться, захлопываться, срабатывать (о пружине))
examples: Old hinges spring back harder than new ones.
The trap sprang the moment he touched the bait.
The screen door had sprung shut behind her.

senses.head: spring up — appear suddenly
body: Of businesses, buildings, rumors, and weeds — things that show up fast and in numbers. Nearly always with up. (возникать, вырастать (как грибы))
examples: New coffee shops have sprung up all over the neighborhood.
Tent cities sprang up along the highway within a week.

senses.head: spring from — originate in
body: Of ideas, movements, or feelings traced back to a source. The same sense covers water issuing from the ground, which is where the noun spring comes from. (происходить из, проистекать из)
examples: The whole project sprang from a conversation at lunch.
Her caution springs from years of being burned.
Two creeks have sprung from that hillside for as long as anyone remembers.

senses.head: spring something on someone
body: Present news, a question, or a demand with no warning — the thing sprung is normally unwelcome. (огорошить, преподнести неожиданно)
examples: She springs the same question on me every year.
They sprang a surprise inspection on the whole department.

senses.head: spring a leak
body: Fixed phrase: start leaking, of a boat, roof, or pipe. Extended to organizations that begin leaking information. (дать течь)
examples: The old boat sprang a leak two miles out.
The roof has sprung a leak over the kitchen again.

senses.head: spring someone — get them released
body: Informal: secure someone's release from jail, a hospital, or anywhere confining. (вызволить, вытащить (из тюрьмы, больницы))
examples: His brother sprang him on bail the same night.
We have sprung her from the clinic a day early.

entries.register: everyday — spring up, spring a leak, and sprang to his feet are all ordinary speech
entries.contrast: Edited American prose prefers sprang for the past — she sprang to her feet — but sprung is widely used in speech and is not an error. The participle is sprung: the trap has sprung. Note the fixed phrase spring a leak, whose past is sprang a leak, and the adjective sprung in the mattress is sprung.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of sudden elastic movement (he sprang out of his chair), of a mechanism releasing (the trap sprang), and of things appearing or originating (coffee shops have sprung up, the project sprang from a conversation). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive in the leap, snap, spring up, and spring from senses, transitive in spring a leak, spring someone (get them released), and spring something on someone (they sprang a surprise inspection on the department).
entries.passive: restricted — natural in the surprise and release senses: a surprise inspection was sprung on the whole department, she was sprung from the clinic a day early. No passive of the intransitive he sprang out of his chair, and the fixed spring a leak resists it: ✗ a leak was sprung by the old boat.
entries.phrasal verbs: spring for · spring on · spring up

entries.meaning: To smell very bad — and, informally, to be very bad indeed.
examples: Those old sneakers stink.
The whole kitchen stank of burnt garlic.
That basement has stunk since the flood.
The trash had stunk for two days before anyone took it out.
Our defense stinks this season.
He said the movie stank, and he was right.
Their last three albums have stunk, and they know it.
The whole deal stinks of a payoff.
The contract stank of favoritism from the first page.
Somebody stank up the break room with fish again.
He has stunk up the joint for three games straight.

senses.head: Smell foul
body: Blunt but not vulgar, and much stronger than smell bad. Both stank and stunk work as the past in American English, with stank the more traditional written choice; the participle is only stunk. (вонять, смердеть)
examples: Those old sneakers stink.
The whole kitchen stank of burnt garlic.
That basement has stunk since the flood.
The trash had stunk for two days before anyone took it out.

senses.head: Be terrible, be no good (informal)
body: Casual American usage about teams, movies, performances, and situations. That stinks is the standard sympathetic reply to someone's bad news. (быть отвратительным, никуда не годиться)
examples: Our defense stinks this season.
He said the movie stank, and he was right.
Their last three albums have stunk, and they know it.

senses.head: stink of — reek of something suspect
body: Figurative: give off a strong impression of corruption, money, or desperation. Always with of. (попахивать, отдавать (чем-то нечистым))
examples: The whole deal stinks of a payoff.
The contract stank of favoritism from the first page.

senses.head: stink up — fill with a bad smell; ruin
body: Literally to fill a room with stench; in sports talk, to play so badly that you spoil the game — stink up the joint. (провонять; испортить, загубить)
examples: Somebody stank up the break room with fish again.
He has stunk up the joint for three games straight.

entries.register: everyday — blunt and casual, but that stinks is constant American speech
entries.contrast: Both stank and stunk serve as the past in American English — the fridge stank and the fridge stunk are both heard, with stank the more traditional choice in writing. The participle is only stunk: it has stunk all week. The -ing form doubles as a casual intensifying adjective: this stinking heat.
entries.verb type: action in form but stative in behavior — it reports an ongoing property (smelling foul, being no good), not an event, so the simple present is the normal tense (those old sneakers stink, our defense stinks this season) and the progressive is rare in American English: ✗ the fridge is stinking.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in every core sense — the whole kitchen stank, the movie stank, and in stink of the of-phrase is a complement, not an object (the deal stinks of a payoff). Only the phrasal stink up takes an object: somebody stank up the break room.
entries.passive: no — the verb is intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the kitchen was stunk, ✗ the movie was stunk by the cast. Only stink up passivizes at all, and even that is marginal and informal: ?the break room was stunk up again, more naturally got stunk up.

entries.meaning: To move through water under your own power — and figuratively to be awash in something, or to feel the world spinning.
examples: I swim laps three mornings a week.
She swam across the lake and back before breakfast.
He has swum competitively since he was six.
She wants to swim the Channel before she turns fifty.
Nobody had swum that stretch of river in years.
The fries came swimming in grease.
The whole plate swam in gravy.
My head swims whenever I stand up too fast.
The room swam for a second and then steadied.
Her head had swum all afternoon before she finally ate something.
New hires here sink or swim.
He has swum against the tide his whole career.

senses.head: Move through water
body: The core sense, of people and animals alike. Swam is the past and swum the participle — ✗ I have swam a mile is the standard error. (плавать, плыть)
examples: I swim laps three mornings a week.
She swam across the lake and back before breakfast.
He has swum competitively since he was six.

senses.head: Cross or cover by swimming
body: Transitive, with the distance or the body of water as the object — swim the Channel, swim two miles. (переплывать, проплывать (дистанцию))
examples: She wants to swim the Channel before she turns fifty.
Nobody had swum that stretch of river in years.

senses.head: Be awash, float in liquid
body: Of food or objects surrounded by far too much liquid, normally swimming in. Extended to being overwhelmed: swimming in paperwork. (плавать в чём-л., быть залитым)
examples: The fries came swimming in grease.
The whole plate swam in gravy.

senses.head: (Of the head or the room) spin
body: Of dizziness — the head swims, or the room swims around you. Common after standing up fast, after a blow, or after too much information. (кружиться (о голове); плыть перед глазами)
examples: My head swims whenever I stand up too fast.
The room swam for a second and then steadied.
Her head had swum all afternoon before she finally ate something.

senses.head: sink or swim / swim against the tide
body: Two fixed phrases: manage entirely on your own with no help, and hold a position against prevailing opinion. (либо выплыть, либо утонуть; идти против течения)
examples: New hires here sink or swim.
He has swum against the tide his whole career.

entries.register: everyday — the ordinary word for moving through water
entries.contrast: Swam is the past and swum the participle. ✗ I have swam a mile is the standard error — the participle is swum: I have swum a mile. Swum is rare enough on its own that speakers reach for swam after have, but only swum is correct there.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, of moving through water (I swim laps three mornings a week) and, figuratively, of being awash (the plate swam in gravy) or feeling dizzy (my head swims). No stative or linking use.
entries.transitivity: both — usually intransitive (she swam across the lake, the room swam for a second), transitive when the distance or the water crossed is the object (swim the Channel, swim two miles, nobody had swum that stretch of river). The object is optional and only appears in that crossing sense.
entries.passive: restricted — possible only in the transitive crossing sense, and mostly in sports writing: that stretch of river hadn't been swum in years, the Channel has been swum by hundreds of people. No passive of the intransitive uses: ✗ the lake was swum across by her, ✗ the room was swum.
